title: Motor Vehicles Act: Duties of driver after accident
citation: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (India)
text: When a road accident occurs, the driver is expected to stop, assist the injured person in obtaining medical care, share identifying information, and report the incident to the police as required by law. Leaving the scene without complying with these duties can trigger criminal and regulatory consequences.

title: Good Samaritan protections and emergency aid
citation: Parmanand Katara v. Union of India (1989) and subsequent Good Samaritan framework
text: Indian legal policy encourages immediate medical assistance to accident victims. A bystander helping an injured person should not be harassed for unnecessary procedural reasons; saving life first is a key legal and constitutional principle.

title: Rash and negligent driving consequences
citation: Indian criminal law principles on rash/negligent driving and causing hurt/death
text: If a person drives rashly or negligently and causes injury or death, criminal prosecution can follow. Punishment can increase with gravity of harm, and courts consider surrounding facts such as speed, conduct after accident, and evidence quality.

title: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal compensation route
citation: Motor Vehicles Act compensation framework (MACT)
text: Victims and dependents can seek monetary compensation through the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal. Key documents usually include FIR details, medical records, proof of income, death/injury proof, and evidence linking accident to the offending vehicle.

title: Sarla Verma compensation principles
citation: Sarla Verma v. Delhi Transport Corporation (2009)
text: The Supreme Court clarified structured principles for calculating compensation in fatal accident claims, including use of income, future prospects in relevant contexts, and multiplier-based assessment for dependency loss.

title: Pranay Sethi on future prospects and conventional heads
citation: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi (2017)
text: The Court refined compensation calculation by standardizing treatment of future prospects and conventional heads such as loss of estate, funeral expenses, and consortium, improving consistency in award determination.

title: Mandatory FIR for cognizable offenses
citation: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh (2013)
text: For cognizable offenses, registration of FIR is generally mandatory. Preliminary inquiry is limited to specific categories and cannot become a routine barrier where law requires immediate registration.

title: Arrest and detention safeguards
citation: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)
text: Arrest and detention must follow constitutional safeguards, including procedural transparency and protection against abuse. Families and legal representatives should be able to trace custody events and documentation.

title: Fair procedure under Article 21
citation: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
text: Any state action affecting life or personal liberty must satisfy fair, just, and reasonable procedure. Arbitrary deprivation is inconsistent with constitutional guarantees.

title: Basic structure doctrine
citation: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
text: Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot destroy its basic structure. This doctrine protects foundational constitutional principles from total abrogation.

title: Right to privacy
citation: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017)
text: Privacy is a fundamental right under the Constitution. State or private intrusions into personal data and autonomy are assessed against legality, necessity, and proportionality standards.

title: Workplace sexual harassment safeguards
citation: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997)
text: Before statutory codification, Vishaka guidelines required institutions to prevent and redress workplace sexual harassment. The legal principle remains that employers must provide a safe and dignified workplace.

title: Free speech and online expression
citation: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)
text: Restrictions on speech must meet constitutional standards. Broad and vague criminalization of online expression was struck down where it disproportionately restricted free speech rights.

title: Arrest caution in matrimonial cruelty cases
citation: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014)
text: The Supreme Court cautioned against automatic arrests and emphasized statutory safeguards, requiring reasoned police action and judicial scrutiny instead of mechanical detention.

title: Landlord-tenant eviction due process
citation: State rent control and tenancy law principles in India
text: A landlord generally cannot forcibly evict a tenant without due legal process. Notice requirements, grounds of eviction, and procedure vary by state rent law and contract terms.

title: Contract breach and remedies
citation: Indian Contract Act, 1872 principles
text: When a contract is breached, remedies may include damages, specific performance in appropriate cases, injunctions, and restitution. Courts examine contract terms, proof of breach, mitigation efforts, and actual loss.

title: Cheque dishonour process
citation: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (Section 138 framework)
text: Cheque dishonour proceedings typically require timely statutory notice and complaint filing within prescribed timelines. Missing limitation windows can affect enforceability.

title: Bail principles in criminal matters
citation: General Indian criminal procedure principles on bail
text: Bail decisions balance personal liberty with investigation and trial interests. Courts often consider gravity of offense, flight risk, witness tampering risk, and cooperation with process.

title: Cyber fraud complaint workflow
citation: Information Technology Act and criminal law complaint practice
text: Victims of online fraud should preserve transaction records, screenshots, account identifiers, and complaint numbers, then report promptly through cyber portals and police channels to improve recovery prospects.

title: Domestic violence civil protections
citation: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
text: Affected persons may seek protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief, and custody-related directions through the statutory mechanism, in addition to applicable criminal remedies.

title: Divorce by mutual consent
citation: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 Section 13B; Special Marriage Act, 1954 Section 28
text: Spouses can seek divorce by mutual consent if they have lived separately for at least one year and mutually agree that the marriage has irretrievably broken down. The court grants a cooling-off period of six months (which can be waived in certain circumstances as per Supreme Court rulings) before passing the final decree. Both parties must file a joint petition and appear before the court.

title: Contested divorce grounds
citation: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 Section 13; Special Marriage Act, 1954 Section 27
text: A spouse may seek divorce on grounds including cruelty (physical or mental), adultery, desertion for a continuous period of not less than two years, conversion to another religion, unsoundness of mind, venereal disease, renunciation of the world, or if the other spouse has not been heard of as alive for seven years. The petitioner must prove the ground before the court.

title: Alimony and maintenance rights
citation: Hindu Marriage Act Section 25; Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act Section 18; CrPC Section 125
text: A spouse (wife or husband in certain cases) can claim maintenance during and after divorce proceedings. Under Section 125 CrPC, a wife, children, and aged parents can claim maintenance from a person with sufficient means who neglects or refuses to maintain them. The court considers factors like income, standard of living, conduct of parties, and duration of marriage. Maintenance can be interim (during proceedings) or permanent (after decree). Non-payment of court-ordered maintenance can lead to attachment of salary, property seizure, and even imprisonment for contempt of court.

title: Consequences of non-payment of alimony
citation: CrPC Section 125(3); Hindu Marriage Act Section 25; Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
text: If a person fails to pay court-ordered alimony or maintenance, the aggrieved spouse can file an execution petition in the family court. The court can order: (1) attachment and sale of the defaulter's property, (2) garnishment of wages/salary, (3) detention in civil prison for up to one month for each default. Under Section 125(3) CrPC, if maintenance is not paid without sufficient cause, the Magistrate can issue a warrant for levying the amount as a fine, and may sentence the defaulter to imprisonment for up to one month or until payment. Repeated non-compliance can also be treated as contempt of court.

title: Child custody and guardianship
citation: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956; Guardians and Wards Act, 1890
text: In custody disputes, the paramount consideration is the welfare and best interests of the child. For Hindu families, the mother is generally the natural guardian of children below five years of age. Courts consider factors including the child's age, gender, wishes of the child (if old enough), moral and material welfare, parent's character, capacity, and living conditions. Joint custody and visitation rights can also be ordered.

title: Dowry demand and harassment
citation: Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961; IPC Section 498A
text: Demanding, giving, or taking dowry is a punishable offense. Cruelty by a husband or his relatives in connection with dowry demands is punishable under Section 498A IPC with imprisonment up to three years and fine. If a woman dies within seven years of marriage under suspicious circumstances related to dowry, it can be treated as dowry death under Section 304B IPC.

title: Property transfer and registration
citation: Transfer of Property Act, 1882; Registration Act, 1908
text: Transfer of immovable property above a certain value must be by a registered instrument (sale deed). The document must be executed on proper stamp paper, registered at the Sub-Registrar's office within the jurisdiction where the property is located, and requires payment of stamp duty and registration fees. Unregistered documents for properties requiring registration cannot be admitted as evidence of the transaction.

title: Hindu succession and inheritance rights
citation: Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as amended in 2005)
text: Under the Hindu Succession Act as amended in 2005, daughters have equal coparcenary rights in ancestral property by birth, similar to sons. If a Hindu dies intestate (without a will), the property devolves upon Class I heirs (including sons, daughters, widow, mother) equally. Self-acquired property can be disposed of by will; if there is no will, it follows the rules of intestate succession.

title: Making a valid will
citation: Indian Succession Act, 1925
text: Any person of sound mind who is not a minor can make a will disposing of their property. A will must be signed by the testator and attested by at least two witnesses. A will can be revoked or altered at any time during the testator's lifetime. Registration of a will is optional but recommended to avoid disputes. A will takes effect only after the death of the testator.

title: Employment termination and wrongful dismissal
citation: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947; Shops and Establishments Acts
text: Termination of employment must follow principles of natural justice, including opportunity to be heard. For workmen under the Industrial Disputes Act, retrenchment requires one month's notice or pay in lieu, retrenchment compensation (15 days' average pay for every year of service), and prior government notification for establishments with 100+ workers. Wrongful termination can be challenged before labor courts or industrial tribunals.

title: Prevention of Sexual Harassment at Workplace
citation: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013
text: Every employer with 10 or more employees must constitute an Internal Complaints Committee. A complaint must be filed within 3 months of the incident (extendable by 3 months). The committee must complete its inquiry within 90 days and submit a report within 10 days thereafter. Penalties for the respondent can include written apology, warning, withholding of promotion, termination, and deduction from salary.

title: Consumer complaint and redressal
citation: Consumer Protection Act, 2019
text: Consumers can file complaints regarding defective goods, deficient services, unfair trade practices, and misleading advertisements. Complaints can be filed at District Commission (up to Rs 1 crore), State Commission (Rs 1 crore to Rs 10 crore), or National Commission (above Rs 10 crore). Complaints can be filed online through the e-daakhil portal. Time limit is generally 2 years from the date of cause of action. Remedies include replacement, refund, compensation, and discontinuation of unfair practices.

title: Right to Information application
citation: Right to Information Act, 2005
text: Any citizen can seek information from public authorities by filing an RTI application with Rs 10 fee. The Public Information Officer must respond within 30 days (48 hours in life/liberty matters). If unsatisfied, first appeal lies to the First Appellate Authority within 30 days, and second appeal to the Information Commission. Personal information of officials related to public duty can be sought under RTI.

title: FIR filing process and rights
citation: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 Section 154
text: For cognizable offenses, police must register an FIR. The informant has a right to a free copy of the FIR. If police refuse to register, a complaint can be made to the Superintendent of Police or a Magistrate under Section 156(3). Zero FIR can be lodged at any police station regardless of jurisdiction. E-FIR facility is available in many states for certain offenses.

title: Anticipatory bail provisions
citation: Code of Criminal Procedure Section 438
text: A person who has reason to believe they may be arrested for a non-bailable offense can apply for anticipatory bail before the Sessions Court or High Court. The court considers the nature of the accusation, antecedents, possibility of fleeing justice, and whether the accusation is made to injure or humiliate. Conditions like surrender of passport, not leaving India, and cooperation with investigation may be imposed.

title: Mediation and alternative dispute resolution
citation: Mediation Act, 2023; Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
text: Mediation offers a voluntary, confidential process where a neutral mediator helps parties reach a mutually acceptable settlement. Under the Mediation Act, 2023, mediated settlement agreements have the force of a court decree. Courts often refer cases to mediation, especially in matrimonial, commercial, and property disputes. Lok Adalats provide free and binding dispute resolution for pending and pre-litigation matters.

title: Cybercrime reporting and remedies
citation: Information Technology Act, 2000; Indian Penal Code provisions
text: Victims of cybercrime can report incidents at cybercrime.gov.in or call 1930 (national cybercrime helpline). For financial fraud, immediate reporting within the 'golden hour' improves recovery chances. Common offenses include online fraud, identity theft, hacking, cyberbullying, and morphing. Evidence preservation (screenshots, transaction records, emails) is critical. Cyber cells in police departments handle specialized investigations.

title: Land mutation and revenue records
citation: State Revenue Codes and Land Revenue Acts
text: After purchasing property, the buyer must apply for mutation (name change) in revenue records at the local Tehsildar or municipal office. Mutation does not confer ownership but reflects the current possessor for tax purposes. Required documents typically include the registered sale deed, previous owner's records, property tax receipts, and identity proof. Revenue records like 7/12 extract (in Maharashtra) or Khata (in Karnataka) serve as important property documents.

title: Rent agreement and tenant rights
citation: State Rent Control Acts; Model Tenancy Act, 2021
text: A written rent agreement is advisable and should specify rent amount, duration, security deposit terms, maintenance responsibilities, and termination conditions. Under most state laws, a landlord cannot increase rent beyond prescribed limits or evict without proper notice and valid grounds. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 recommends a written agreement, security deposit cap of 2 months' rent, and establishment of Rent Authorities and Rent Tribunals for dispute resolution.

title: Gratuity payment rights
citation: Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972
text: Employees who have completed 5 years of continuous service are entitled to gratuity upon retirement, resignation, death, or disablement. The amount is calculated as 15 days' wages for every completed year of service (7 days for seasonal workers). Maximum limit is Rs 20 lakh (as of recent amendment). Gratuity is payable within 30 days of it becoming due. In case of delay, interest is payable. The employer cannot forfeit gratuity except in cases of termination for moral turpitude or violent conduct.

title: Provident Fund and EPF withdrawal
citation: Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952
text: EPF contributions are mandatory for establishments with 20+ employees. Both employer and employee contribute 12% of basic salary. PF can be withdrawn fully after retirement at 58, or partially for specific purposes like home purchase, medical emergency, or education. After leaving a job, PF can be transferred to the new employer or withdrawn after 2 months of unemployment. UAN (Universal Account Number) allows online management of PF accounts.

title: Motor vehicle insurance claim process
citation: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988; IRDAI guidelines
text: After a vehicle accident, the insured should inform the insurer within the time specified in the policy (usually 24-48 hours), file an FIR for third-party claims, not authorize repairs without surveyor's inspection, and submit the claim form with supporting documents (RC, license, FIR, repair estimates, photos). Third-party liability insurance is mandatory. Own-damage claims are subject to policy terms. MACT (Motor Accident Claims Tribunal) handles compensation disputes.

title: Assault and criminal force
citation: Indian Penal Code Sections 349-358
text: Using criminal force or assault against any person is punishable. Simple hurt can attract imprisonment up to one year. Grievous hurt (fracture, permanent disfigurement, etc.) can attract imprisonment up to seven years. If weapons are used, punishment is more severe. The victim should file an FIR immediately, get a medico-legal certificate (MLC) from the hospital, and preserve any evidence like CCTV footage or witness statements.

title: Defamation laws
citation: Indian Penal Code Sections 499-502; Civil defamation principles
text: Making or publishing false statements that harm someone's reputation can be both a criminal offense (punishable with up to 2 years imprisonment) and a civil wrong (actionable for damages). Truth is a defense if the statement was made in public interest. Exceptions include fair comment, privileged communication, and statements made in good faith. Online defamation is also actionable under both criminal and IT laws.

title: Marriage registration
citation: Hindu Marriage Act Section 8; Special Marriage Act; State Marriage Registration Rules
text: Marriage registration is advisable though not mandatory for validity of Hindu marriages. Under the Special Marriage Act, registration is part of the marriage process itself. Registration requires application to the Marriage Registrar with documents including age proof, address proof, photographs, and witnesses. A marriage certificate serves as conclusive proof of marriage for passport, visa, insurance, and other official purposes.
